 Army veteran Terrance Adams lived in his Dodge Charger for 8 months due to a credit score in the 500s — then hit 756
 Vawn Himmelsbach Sun, November 15, 2026 at 11:30 AM CST 7 min read prostooleh/Envato Terrance Adams, an Army Reserve veteran, was working full-time, but for eight months he lived out of his Dodge Charger — not because he couldn't afford rent, but because his credit score was preventing him from literally getting a foot in the door.

 If you have a low credit score, landlords might request a larger security deposit, prepaid rent or a guarantor with good credit to co-sign the lease. 
 "They're asking me for three times the rent," he told MarketWatch . "They're asking the co-signer to make five times the rent." 
 Adams hadn't realized his credit score had dropped into the 500s — giving him a 'poor' rating. When shopping for a new car, he discovered that the women he had been in a relationship with at the time had been using his credit. 
 Fast forward to October, and Adams has a credit score of 756, bought a new car and signed a lease for his own place. Here's how he did it. 
 Understanding your credit score 
 For Adams, the turning point came when he discovered Soldier On, a nonprofit that aims to end veteran homelessness. The organization put him in touch with Money Management International, where a financial counselor worked with him to repair his credit profile. 
 Part of this process involved finding a higher-paying job to boost his income. But the financial counselor also helped him dispute incorrect charges on his profile and link his accounts so on-time bill payments would be reported to the credit bureaus. 
 Six months later, he had a score of 756 — opening the door to more financial freedom. 
 There are three major credit bureaus in the U.S.: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Your credit score may be slightly different at each of the bureaus, since not all lenders report to all three bureaus. 
 Lenders use this information when deciding whether to approve you for financing such as credit cards, auto loans, mortgages, personal loans and student loans. 
 "Your credit report may also be used by insurance providers to help them determine policy rates, landlords for rental screening , and even employers for a background check when permitted by law," according to TransUnion. 
 Story Continues Basically, by analyzing your credit history, they're weighing factors to determine how likely you are to pay back your loan. This not only affects whether you get a loan, but how much you'll pay for it. And a lower score typically means a higher rate. 
 The FICO model ranks 579 or less as poor, 580 to 669 as fair, 670 to 739 as good, 740 to 799 as very good and 800+ as excellent. 
 A poor score means you've likely defaulted on past loans, which indicates you're a higher risk for lenders. While a good score means you're more likely to qualify for standard loans and competitive interest rates, a very good or excellent score gives you access to better rates and more favorable terms.

 Why you should check your credit score 
 It's a good idea to check your credit score regularly so you're not caught off guard if there's an issue. If you notice an error on your credit report, file a dispute with the credit bureau in question (it's a bit of a process , but the credit bureaus are required to investigate and report back to you). 
 And it happens more often than you might think: a 2024 survey by Consumer Reports found that 44% of respondents found at least one error in their credit reports, including 27% who found an error relating to debt information. 
 Plus, it could help you spot identity theft, which could cause severe damage to your credit score. For example, if someone steals your identity, they could get a credit card in your name. Then, when they don't pay the bill, the account is reported as delinquent — on your credit report. 
 You can review your credit reports for free through AnnualCreditReport.com. 
 If you're unaware that your credit score has dropped, you may find yourself paying higher rates than you would otherwise qualify for — or, in a worst-case scenario, find yourself sleeping in your truck because landlords slam the door in your face. 
 How to boost your credit score 
 If your credit score is holding you back, there are steps you can take — like Adams did — to boost your score. 
 "You can't be a passive passenger to your own credit story," Adams told MarketWatch. "You have more power than you think." 
 One way you can boost your score is by linking household bill payments — such as utility, cellphone, cable, internet, streaming, insurance and rent — to your credit file. Experian does this in-house through Experian Boost , while TransUnion uses the Credit Spark platform. 
 Normally those bill payments wouldn't factor into your overall credit score, since they're not traditionally reported to the credit bureaus. But if you link your accounts — and if you pay your bills on time — it could help to rebuild your credit score. 
 Other ways to rebuild your credit and establish a positive payment history include using a secured credit card (where you provide a cash deposit upfront that serves as your credit limit) or using a credit-builder loan (where you make monthly payments, which are reported to the credit bureaus, and then receive the money plus interest after paying the loan off in full). 
 Your repayment history plays a key role in establishing your credit score. That means you want to pay your loans on time, every time. 
 At the very least, make the minimum payment on time each month. You can set up electronic reminders or even automatic payments to make this easier to remember. Ideally, you want to get to a point where you can pay off the balance in full each month. 
 Also try to keep your credit utilization in check. A general rule of thumb is to use no more than 30% of your total credit limit; if you're too close to your limit, lenders may view you as more high risk. 
 If you're deep in debt, you might benefit from some professional assistance. Vets can reach out to an organization like Soldier On, while civilians can search for non-profit credit counseling services through the National Foundation for Credit Counseling (NFCC), some of which are free or partially free.
